Adult sand perch (Diplectrum formosum) collected off the southeastern coast of the United States routinely attain a maximum length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm], a size that represents the upper extreme of the species' asymptotic body length. Individuals reach this ultimate total length through a growth trajectory that appears tightly linked to the thermal regime of their habitat. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 25.2 °C [T = 25.2 °C], fertilised eggs proceed through embryonic development and yolk-sac absorption relatively quickly, with the first free-swimming larvae emerging from the chorion just 7 days [ab = 7 days] after fertilisation. This brief embryonic period, equivalent to a single week of development, places the species among the faster-hatching members of the Serranidae. The hatchlings, still reliant on endogenous yolk reserves, emerge at a remarkably small size; the wet weight at birth measured from these laboratory-reared individuals is a mere 0.000344 grams [Wwb = 0.000344 grams], a value that underscores the extremely altricial condition of the newly emerged pelagic larva. Such minimal neonatal mass imposes a narrow window for the onset of exogenous feeding once the yolk is fully resorbed.

The transition to sexual maturity in Diplectrum formosum is marked by predictable milestones in both length and body mass. Puberty, defined here as the onset of gonadal recrudescence and incipient gametogenesis, is attained when individuals reach approximately 12.9 cm [Lp = approximately 12.9 cm] in total length. At this point, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is roughly 25.3 grams [Wwp = roughly 25.3 grams], a mass that reflects the energetic investment required to support the first wave of vitellogenesis or spermatogenesis. Field surveys indicate that a substantial proportion of individuals collected from the eastern Gulf of Mexico exceed this size threshold by their second year of life, though growth rates vary with local food availability and bottom temperature. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a steep allometric curve, exemplified by the fact that a fish at the pubertal length of 12.9 cm weighs about 25.3 grams [Wwp = about 25.3 grams], whereas an individual nearing its ultimate length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm] weighs an order of magnitude more. Such a dramatic gain in mass per unit length is characteristic of robust, deeper-bodied serranids.

Peak reproductive output in the sand perch is considerable when considered on an annual scale. Gravid females held in aquaria at a stable water temperature of 25.2 °C [T = 25.2 °C] and fed to satiation were observed to produce approximately 13,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 13,000 eggs per year], a rate that translates to a substantial cumulative fecundity over the course of a reproductive period. Extrapolating from daily egg production and assuming that spawning occurs on most days during the season yields an annual fecundity on the order of several thousand eggs per female. The annual rate of egg output itself, recorded consistently under controlled thermal conditions at 25.2 °C [T = 25.2 °C], appears tightly coupled to maternal size, with larger females contributing disproportionately more to the year's cohort. Although the daily egg count is modest compared to some batch-spawning pelagic spawners, the extended spawning season of this warm-temperate serranid ensures that lifetime fecundity remains competitive within its guild. The reproductive biology thus reflects an iteroparous strategy where females spread reproductive effort across many days.

Maximum adult body size in Diplectrum formosum is reflected not only in length but also in mass, with fully grown individuals reaching an ultimate wet weight of 346 grams [Wwi = 346 grams]. This asymptotic mass is attained gradually over several years as growth decelerates approaching the upper size limit. The relationship between length and mass used to derive this value follows the general power law common among teleosts, where weight scales approximately as the cube of length, but with a slightly steeper exponent indicative of robust body shape. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty of 25.3 grams [Wwp = 25.3 grams] represents a mere fraction of the maximum attainable body mass, meaning that individuals begin investing energy in reproduction while still growing rapidly. This early onset of maturity relative to ultimate size is common in short-lived, fast-growing serranids and likely reflects selective pressure to reproduce before mortality risks accumulate. The lifespan of the sand perch under natural conditions has been estimated from otolith-based age validation studies to be approximately 24 years [am = approximately 24 years] when maintained at a typical ambient temperature of 25.2 °C [T = 25.2 °C], a longevity that is moderate among reef-associated serranids.

Otolith-based aging studies place the maximum recorded longevity of the sand perch at around 24 years [am = around 24 years] under the prevailing thermal regime of 25.2 °C [T = 25.2 °C]. This life span is notably longer than that of many small-bodied serranids and may be linked to the species' relatively deep-water habitat, which avoids the high predation pressure characteristic of shallow reef zones. The extended life span, coupled with a growth trajectory that slows markedly after the attainment of a total length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm], suggests a life history strategy that balances early reproductive investment against the potential for repeated spawning across many seasons. The size at which females first reproduce corresponds to a total length of 12.9 cm [Lp = 12.9 cm], and the wet weight at that maturational milestone, 25.3 grams [Wwp = 25.3 grams], is consistent with values derived from length-weight regressions for other Gulf of Mexico serranids. Overall, the species exhibits a stable life history that appears well matched to the relatively predictable, warm-temperate conditions of its continental shelf environment.
